Seif katan 7, "and some say," etc. Tosafos in Pesachim discuss the eve of Pesach that fell on Shabbos. One who forgot to bring a knife to the Temple courtyard for slaughtering his Pesach offering could not carry it normally in Jerusalem. The Mishnah therefore teaches that one whose offering was a lamb stuck the knife into its wool, and one whose offering was a goat placed it between its horns. The Gemara asks that he is driving an animal carrying a burden, and answers that this is driving in an unusual manner, because a lamb or goat does not ordinarily carry a load. Tosafos write that the Gemara could have answered that when the animal walks he places the knife upon it, and when it stops he removes it, in the same manner permitted at the beginning of Perek Mi SheHechshich.

Eliyah Rabbah and Chemed Moshe ask what proof can be brought from there against Rambam. Tosafos merely say that the case is like the permitted case at the beginning of Perek Mi SheHechshich. According to Rambam, that earlier case can be understood where the owner does not lead the animal by his voice, and the same could be done with the Pesach offering.

In my humble opinion there is no difficulty. An animal does not understand on its own where its owner wishes it to go. At times it stands in place and will not move until its owner compels it by calling, striking, or the like. In the case at the beginning of Perek Mi SheHechshich, Rambam holds that one was not permitted to lead it by voice. If the animal refuses to walk, nothing further need be permitted, because the Sages did not permit more. With a Pesach offering, however, if the animal stands still and does not go to the Temple courtyard, how will its owner fulfill the mitzvah? He will inevitably have to raise his voice and force it to move. According to Rambam that is forbidden. The Gemara's answer that the burden is carried in an unusual manner is therefore preferable. This shows that Tosafos disagree with Rambam on this point.

"Hagahot Mordechai writes," etc., that one who rides an animal violates only a rabbinic prohibition, namely the decree against riding. He does not violate the mitzvah of allowing his animal to rest because a living person carries himself. Likewise, the saddle does not create a violation of the animal's rest because the saddle is secondary to the rider, as stated in Shabbos 93b.

"According to Rambam it appears," etc., "and he should throw," etc. Accordingly it is better for him to go on foot, because then he performs no prohibition at all when the animal is not carrying a burden. There is neither a violation of the animal's rest nor of driving an animal carrying a load. If he rides, by contrast, he violates the rabbinic decree against riding.

"And perhaps it is better to ride," etc. These are Beit Yosef's words added to Hagahot Mordechai, which dealt with a case within the techum. Beit Yosef introduces a possible leniency where one must leave the techum.

The basis is the unresolved question in Eruvin 43a whether the laws of techumin apply above 10 tefachim. "Regarding riding we rule leniently," meaning that the rider's place upon the animal is above 10 tefachim.

"However," etc., "beyond 12 mil," etc. This follows Rambam's view, cited below in siman 404, that techumin beyond 12 mil are a Torah prohibition.

The correct text is: "Beyond 12 mil, perhaps it is better," etc. Within 12 mil, techumin are rabbinic, so we rule leniently in the doubt whether techumin apply above 10 tefachim. One might ask: what difference is there between riding and walking? If he walks, he still violates only a rabbinic techum prohibition, and riding is actually worse because it adds the rabbinic prohibition against riding. Therefore within 12 mil it is preferable to walk. Beyond 12 mil, however, according to Rambam walking may violate a Torah prohibition. Riding may then be preferable because, being above 10 tefachim, he can invoke the unresolved question concerning techumin above 10 tefachim. In a Torah-level doubt we cannot simply rule leniently, but the balance between the prohibitions is different, and the authorities analyze which course is preferable.

One must also consider that riding can involve leading the animal by voice, which according to Rambam constitutes a separate prohibition. If the animal can proceed without his directing it, that concern does not arise. If it will not move without his voice, this affects the analysis, as explained above from the Pesach case.

The general rule emerging from the discussion is that when a person is faced with possible violation of techum, riding, driving an animal, and the animal's required rest, one must distinguish between a Torah-level and rabbinic techum, between travel below and above 10 tefachim, whether the animal carries an independent burden or only the rider and what is secondary to him, and whether the rider must actively lead the animal by voice. These distinctions determine whether walking, riding, or the method of placing and removing the burden while the animal moves is preferable.
